chunks.title: The strategy, explained
chunks.text:
How this bot makes (and loses) money, in plain language. No code knowledge needed. For the technical side, see the README.

> ## ⚠️ Disclaimer
>
> **This is a study project, not investment advice and not a professional trading tool.**
>
> optionsBot is a personal exercise in Go concurrency and software design that happens to run against a real crypto-derivatives exchange (Deribit). Every number in this document is **illustrative**: rounded, simplified and not a forecast.
>
> - **Selling options can lose many times the premium collected.** A single violent move can erase months of small gains.
> - **Crypto markets are extremely volatile**, trade 24/7 and can gap through any stop-loss.
> - **Past or backtested results do not predict future results.** The backtests in this repository run on synthetic data.
> - The bot runs on **Deribit testnet (play money) by default**. Running it with real money is entirely your own decision and risk.
>
> Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell anything.

chunks.title: 1. The idea in one paragraph
chunks.text: The bot acts like an **insurance seller**. It sells options that pay off only if Bitcoin (or Ether) makes a big move up *or* down within the next few weeks. Buyers pay a fee (the **premium**) up front. Most of the time the big move doesn't come, the options expire worthless or are bought back cheaply, and the bot keeps most of the premium. Sometimes the big move does come, and then the bot must pay out, often much more than it collected. The whole craft is in choosing *how far away* to sell, *when to take profits*, *when to cut losses* and *when to stand aside*.

chunks.title: 2. Options in five minutes
chunks.text:
| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| **Call option** | the right to *buy* BTC at a fixed price (the **strike**) on a date. It gains value when BTC rises above the strike. |
| **Put option** | the right to *sell* BTC at the strike. It gains value when BTC falls below the strike. |
| **Premium** | the price of the option. The **seller** receives it and takes on the obligation. |
| **Expiry / DTE** | the date the option ends; *DTE* = days to expiry. |
| **Strangle** | selling one call *above* today's price and one put *below* it, same expiry. The seller profits if BTC stays between the two strikes. |
| **Delta (Δ)** | roughly, the market's estimate of the chance the option ends up "in the money". A 0.16-delta option is ≈16 % likely to pay out, so ≈84 % likely to expire worthless. |
| **Theta (Θ)** | time decay: how much value the option loses per day. Sellers *earn* theta. It speeds up in the last weeks. |
| **Gamma (Γ)** | how fast delta changes when the price moves. Sellers are *short gamma*: losses accelerate in big moves, especially close to expiry. |
| **Implied volatility (IV)** | how big a move the market is pricing in. Higher IV means higher premiums, and usually more risk. |

chunks.title: 2. Options in five minutes
chunks.text: **Why sell options at all?** Historically, the volatility priced into options has tended to be *higher* than the volatility that actually follows (the "volatility risk premium"). Option buyers overpay for protection on average, and a disciplined seller collects that difference. "On average" hides the problem: the losing periods are rare but large.

chunks.title: 2. Options in five minutes › The payoff of a short strangle at expiry
chunks.text: *Illustrative: BTC at $100,000. Sell 0.1 BTC of the 88k put and 0.1 BTC of the 115k call for a total of about $270. Any expiry price between 88k and 115k keeps the full $270. The break-evens are about $85,300 and $117,700. Beyond them, the loss grows by $100 for every $1,000 BTC moves. There is no cap.*

chunks.title: 3. What the bot does, step by step
chunks.text:
1. **Wakes up and checks the facts.** On every start it asks Deribit what positions actually exist and rebuilds its own records from that. The exchange is always the source of truth.
2. **Fills its "slots".** The configuration lists slots such as *"a strangle about 25 days out at 0.16 delta"* and *"one 50 days out at 0.16 delta"* (BTC: 25 and 50 days; ETH: 30 and 50 — two slots since 2026-10-11: in the stress test two slots beat three, mostly because the third, 60-day slot found no listed expiry in its window much of the time and held the least-earning margin). For each empty slot it:
   - picks the listed expiry closest to the target number of days (never one that is already due to be rolled);
   - picks the call and put strikes together: both near the target delta (e.g.

chunks.title: 3. What the bot does, step by step
3. What the bot does, step by step
chunks.text:
4. **Reads market structure.** It estimates how option dealers are positioned (*gamma exposure*, GEX). When dealers are likely to *amplify* moves (negative gamma) and the trend is clearly down, it stops selling puts and closes existing ones, because that's the side under threat. Calls get the same treatment in a confirmed up-trend.
5. **Even legs.** A strangle is only roughly direction-neutral when both legs have the same size. If they don't — one leg filled only partly, or an order filled twice — the bot buys back the extra on the larger side right away (it reduces risk, so it does this even while new entries are frozen). A difference left by an exit that is filling in pieces is not an uneven strangle: the bot lets that exit finish first (up to 30 min after its last piece once the exit's rule stops firing).

chunks.title: 3. What the bot does, step by step
chunks.text:
6. **Repairs.** If a strangle has lost one leg (rolled, or only one leg filled), it re-sells the missing leg at the same expiry and size, unless the market regime says that side is dangerous. A leg lost to a **stop-loss** is different: the market just moved hard against it, and selling it again at once sells into the same move. It waits until the market is calm again — no regime change pending, dealers not amplifying moves, and at least 3 days since the stop. In a two-week stress simulation (BTC −25 % and +31 %) this kept about 0.05–0.07 BTC that the immediate re-sale lost.
7. **Keeps a decision diary.** Every order, fill, close and skipped opportunity is written down together with the market at that moment: BTC price, the volatility index (DVOL), whether the option was in or out of the money and by how much, how much open interest sat at that strike, and the dealer-positioning regime. Every minute it also writes the profit and loss of each slot, realised and open. This is what lets you judge, afterwards, which settings earn money and under which conditions.

chunks.title: 3. What the bot does, step by step
chunks.text: 8. **Reports, never hedges.** If the book's overall directional exposure (net delta) grows large, it writes a hedge suggestion file. A human decides whether to act on it.

chunks.title: 4. How a trade can end
chunks.text: The rules are checked in this order. The first one that applies wins.

chunks.title: 4. How a trade can end
chunks.text:
| Priority | Rule | Trigger (shipped config) | What the bot does |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Stop-loss** | the leg's loss reaches **2× the premium** received for it | buys it back **at market**, immediately, ahead of all other traffic; if the book is empty (ask more than 20 % above mid) it waits up to 5 minutes for the spread, re-checking each cycle |
| 2 | **Time roll** | **15 days** or fewer left | buys the leg back; once both legs are gone the slot reopens further out |
| 3 | **Delta drift** | the leg's delta falls below **0.10** (far from the price, little premium left) | buys it back; repair re-sells a fresh leg at the target delta, same expiry |
| 4 | **Take-profit** | **50 %** of the leg's premium is captured | buys it back; repair re-sells a fresh leg |
| — | **Regime shed** | negative dealer gamma + confirmed trend, with spot more than about one and a half normal days' move (1.5σ) below the gamma flip, on two snapshots in a row | closes the threatened side at market; it is sold again only once the price is back above the flip it was shed at (plus 1.5σ), or dealer gamma has been non-negative for a day |
| — | **Kill switch** | operator signal | cancels everything, buys back everything at market, then stops trading |

chunks.title: 4. How a trade can end
chunks.text:
How each exit buys back (#239):

| Exit | First | Then |
|---|---|---|
| Stop-loss, MM cut, kill switch | market | — |
| Delta exit, GEX shed, leg balancing, rebalance downsize | as today: delta exit and balancing an immediate-or-cancel limit at the ask, the others at market | retried next cycle |
| **Take-profit, delta drift, time roll** | a buy limit **resting at the mid** (rounded down a tick) for one fill window (90 s, the entries' window) | whatever is left: an immediate-or-cancel limit at the ask of that moment, retried next cycle |

chunks.title: 4. How a trade can end
chunks.text: The three non-urgent exits are not a race, so they first try to save about half the spread. Without a two-sided quote (no bid) or with no tick of room under the ask, they cross at the ask at once. While the order rests, the leg keeps every other exit: a stop-loss, a delta exit, the MM cut, a GEX shed, a manual close or the kill switch cancels the resting order, books what it filled, and runs at once on what is left. If the rule no longer applies when the window ends (the price came back), nothing is bought at the ask. The journal marks the close's `exit_step` (`mid` or `ask`) and its detail gives the price and the bid / mid / ask at the trigger. Stop-losses do not wait for a good price.

chunks.title: 5. Worked examples: wins
chunks.text: All examples: BTC starts at **$100,000**, size **0.1 BTC per leg**. On Deribit, BTC options are priced in BTC; dollar figures use the BTC price at the time and are rounded.

chunks.title: 5. Worked examples: wins › Win A: calm market, take-profit
chunks.text:
- **Day 0:** sell the 45-day 115k call at 0.012 BTC and the 88k put at 0.015 BTC. Premium = (0.012 + 0.015) × 0.1 = **0.0027 BTC ≈ $270**.
- **Day 18:** BTC drifts to $102,000; time decay has done its work. Call worth 0.007 (42 % captured, not yet), put 0.007. The put has captured (0.015 − 0.007) / 0.015 = 53 % ≥ 50 %, so the **take-profit fires**. It's bought back for 0.0007 BTC and books **+0.0008 BTC ≈ +$82**.
- The bot then **re-sells a fresh put** at ≈0.16 delta on the same expiry, collecting new premium. The call keeps decaying until its own rule fires.

chunks.title: 5. Worked examples: wins › Win B: time roll
chunks.text:
- **Day 30** (15 days left): BTC at $97,000. Call 0.002, put 0.006. The **time roll** closes both legs, costing (0.002 + 0.006) × 0.1 = 0.0008 BTC. Net on the strangle: 0.0027 − 0.0008 = **+0.0019 BTC ≈ +$185**.
- The slot is free again, so a new 45-day strangle is opened at today's prices. The bot never holds into the final, most dangerous weeks.

chunks.title: 5. Worked examples: wins › Win C: the far leg goes quiet
chunks.text: - BTC rallies to $108,000. The put drifts far out of the money; its delta falls to 0.07. **Delta drift** closes it for almost nothing and re-sells a new put at 0.16 delta, closer to today's price, collecting fresh premium. The book stays balanced instead of becoming a lone short call.

chunks.title: 6. Worked examples: losses › Loss A: sharp drop, stop-loss
chunks.text:
- **Day 0:** same strangle (put 88k sold at 0.015 BTC).
- **Day 6:** BTC falls 18 % to $82,000 and IV jumps. The put is now worth 0.045 BTC: **3× what was received**, a loss of 2× the premium.
- **Stop-loss fires:** buy back 0.1 put at market ≈ 0.045 → loss on the put = (0.045 − 0.015) × 0.1 = **−0.0030 BTC ≈ −$246**. The call has collapsed to ~0.002 (83 % captured), so its take-profit closes it for **+0.0010 BTC**.
- **Net ≈ −0.0020 BTC ≈ −$164.** That one move erased the profit of about two calm cycles.
- *Crypto twist:* the account's collateral is BTC, so the 18 % drop *also* shrank the account's dollar value. A short put on an inverse (BTC-settled) option loses twice in a crash.

chunks.title: 6. Worked examples: losses › Loss B: gap through the stop
chunks.text:
- A weekend headline sends BTC from $95,000 to $78,000 in an hour. By the time the stop-loss order fills, the put is at 0.06 instead of 0.045.
- Loss on the put = (0.06 − 0.015) × 0.1 = **−0.0045 BTC**, which is 3× the premium, not 2×. **Stop-loss levels are triggers, not guaranteed prices.**

chunks.title: 6. Worked examples: losses › Loss C: whipsaw
chunks.text:
- In a choppy range BTC drops, the regime turns negative, and puts are closed at a loss. Then BTC rebounds, puts are re-sold lower, and BTC drops again.
- Each step is small, but together they bleed. This is why regime changes use a hysteresis band and require a *confirmed* trend before acting.

chunks.title: 6. Worked examples: losses › Loss D: the slow grind
chunks.text:
- BTC trends steadily up 30 % over two months. The call side keeps getting stopped or rolled at a loss, and re-sold closer to the price each time.
- No single loss is large, but the strategy has "sold the rally" again and again. Short strangles do best in ranges and worst in persistent trends.

chunks.title: 7. Edge cases the bot handles
chunks.text:
| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Only one leg fills** before the entry times out | the filled leg is kept and tracked (it is a real short on the exchange) and the other is cancelled; repair later sells the missing leg |
| **Partial fill** (e.g. 0.1 of 0.3 BTC) | the bot records exactly what filled, never the amount it asked for |
| **A close only partly fills** (thin market) | the remainder stays tracked, with its stop-loss, and the rule fires again next cycle |
| **A roll's price-capped buy doesn't fill** | nothing is reopened; the position stays protected and it retries |
| **Internet / exchange drops** | in-flight requests fail fast; the bot reconnects and re-subscribes; if it cannot, it shuts down so the supervisor restarts it, and on start it rebuilds positions from the exchange |
| **Restart with orders resting** | it cancels this currency's stale orders and reloads the positions |
| **Exchange overloaded** | non-urgent traffic pauses (circuit breaker); stop-losses and the kill switch still go through |
| **Order rejected for a too-low price** | it retries once at the exchange's stated minimum |
| **No bid on testnet** | it prices from the ask / mark price instead of zero |

chunks.title: 7. Edge cases the bot handles
chunks.text:
| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| **API key lacks permission** | trading pauses for a minute at a time instead of spamming errors |
| **Kill switch** | resting orders are cancelled first, every position is bought back at market (retrying partial fills), then the bot idles. It does not exit, because Docker would restart it straight back into trading |

chunks.title: 8. Risk controls
chunks.text:
- **Margin limit that follows the market:** the share of the account used as initial margin depends on volatility. When DVOL is high (rich premium, fear already priced in) up to 50 % is allowed; in the middle, 35 %; when it is low (cheap premium, often the calm before a big move), 20 %. When dealer positioning amplifies moves (negative gamma), 20 % applies whatever DVOL says. Every number is Deribit's own margin calculation, including a simulation of each new trade before it is placed.
- **No knee-jerk reactions:** a change of volatility band or gamma regime must hold for two daily closes before the bot resizes anything. Until then it simply stops opening new positions; if the change reverts (a one-day spike), it carries on as before.
- **Distance to liquidation:** if maintenance margin reaches 35 % of the account's margin balance (Deribit liquidates at 100 %), positions are bought back at once, whatever else is going on.
- **Stop-loss on every leg:** 2× premium by default, executed at market with top priority; while the book is empty (ask more than 20 % above mid, a flash wick) it waits up to 5 minutes for the spread to normalise, re-checking each cycle.

chunks.title: 8. Risk controls
chunks.text:
- **Time exit:** nothing is held into the last ~15 days, when gamma risk is highest.
- **Regime filter:** sheds the threatened side when dealer positioning amplifies moves.
- **Premium floor:** refuses to sell options too cheap to justify their risk.
- **Validation:** nonsensical settings (deltas ≥ 0.5, slots inside the roll window, margin limits outside 0–100 %, no stop-loss) stop the bot at startup.
- **Testnet by default; live only on explicit opt-in.**
- **What is *not* covered:** the strangle has no long "wings", and the bot does not hedge automatically, so in a gap the loss is not capped. Covered alternatives, such as iron condors and delta hedging with perpetual futures, are the natural next research step.

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text:
Every rule that opens, closes or holds a position, by market state. **This table is kept up to date with every rule change**; if the code and the table disagree, the code is wrong or the table is late, and either is a bug.

**The states** (more than one can apply at once; the strictest cell wins):

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text:
- **Normal:** the confirmed volatility band and gamma regime are unchanged, and the regime is not negative.
- **Change pending (freeze):** the DVOL band or the gamma regime changed but has not yet held for 2 daily closes (`iv_band_confirm_days`), **and confirming it would lower the margin limit**. New risk is frozen until it is confirmed, or until it reverts. A change that cannot lower the limit only shows as pending, because the current, stricter limit applies until it confirms: a DVOL band rise, a DVOL band change under a confirmed negative regime (the limit is pinned to the lowest band anyway), or the regime turning positive. The regime turning **negative** always freezes, even when the limit stays: it is a danger signal on its own (2026-10-15: ETH sat frozen for three days, flat, on a DVOL change that could not lift its pinned 20 % limit; 2026-10-16: ETH frozen about 8 h of 12 while the live regime flapped to positive, a change that could only lift it — #105).

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text: - **Confirmed negative regime:** the gamma regime has been negative for 2 daily closes. The margin limit drops to the lowest band (20 %), and in a trend the side the price runs toward is not sold: no new puts in a down-trend, no new calls in an up-trend (dealers short gamma push the price further the way it is going). With no trend both sides are sold. When the trend turns toward a side, every entry, repair or top-up still working on that side is cancelled at once (`regime_side`; what filled before the cancel is kept). The SMA trend reads the price against SMA9 with a band of 0.10 daily σ (DVOL ÷ √365, about 0.2–0.3 % of the price) around it: the price changes side of SMA9 only once it is past the band, so spot sitting on SMA9 no longer flips the trend every 40-second cycle (#243: on 2026-10-20 ETH logged 31 trend changes, and a put repair sent in a one-cycle blip filled 100 lots in a bear trend). Measured on a week of minute snapshots, the band cut the trend changes 83–92 % and still followed every lasting change within 8–12 minutes.

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text:
- **GEX shedding a side:** a live 60-second signal. The regime is negative, spot is more than 1 daily σ (DVOL ÷ √365) below the gamma flip, and there is a trend: puts are shed in a down-trend, calls in an up-trend. The close itself waits for the signal to hold on 2 snapshots in a row.
- **MM limit:** maintenance margin is at or above 35 % of the margin balance (`max_mm_pct`).

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text: - **Direction (trend vs bias):** "the trend" above is the SMA trend of daily closes (`gex_direction: sma`, what the bots trade on). The bot also computes the GEX **bias** — spot more than 1.5σ above the flip in a negative regime is "bias up", more than 1.5σ below is "bias down", otherwise neutral — and records both, with what each would shed, so they can be compared on live data. With `gex_direction: bias` the bias replaces the trend in every rule of this table, a rally through the flip sheds calls, and a shed leg is re-sold 24 h after the shed once the bias has left its side. The bias counts only when it points the same way against the live flip and against the median flip of the last hour: in the hours before a daily expiry the flip can jump far from spot for a few minutes, and on 2026-10-12 and 10-14 such a jump read as a rally and shed every BTC call while the price stood still. That hour is kept in memory, so after a restart the bias sheds nothing until it has a full hour of flips behind it (journaled `bias_warmup`; new sales of the side it points to still wait): on 2026-10-14 a jump ten minutes after a restart filled the short window by itself and shed BTC's calls.

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text:
A real move is shed up to an hour late; stop-losses and delta exits protect the legs meanwhile. Stress-tested on 2026-10-12 the bias shed 3–5× as often and returned 16–139 % less than the trend; BTC trades on it as a live trial since 2026-10-12, ETH stays on the trend as the control.
- **No fresh GEX data:** the first minute after a start (before the first GEX snapshot), or the last snapshot is more than 5 minutes old. The regime and trend are unknown, so the bot cannot tell which side is safe to sell.

| **Repair after a stop-loss or delta exit** | ✅ after 72 h (`repair_cooldown_hours`) | ⛔ held (`repair_held`) | ⛔ held | ⛔ for the shed side | ⛔ |
| **Top-up while a slot's leg is held after a stop-loss or manual close** | ⛔ that slot's top-up waits until the repair may run (`repair_held`: top-up held); a strangle missing a leg is never topped up, repair completes it | same | same | same | same |
| **Repair after a GEX shed** | ⛔ held until spot is back above the flip *at the shed* + 1.5σ on 2 snapshots, or the live regime has been non-negative for 24 h | same | same | ⛔ | ⛔ |
| **Balance legs** (buy back the excess of the larger leg) | ✅ · not while the smaller leg is being closed (a roll filling in pieces, a waiting stop), nor while either leg is part-way through an exit (one piece of a roll, delta exit or stop filled: it waits while the exit's rule fires, and 30 min after the last piece once it stops) | ✅ (it reduces risk) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text:
| What the bot does | Normal | Change pending (freeze) | Confirmed negative regime | GEX shedding a side | MM limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Entry and top-up at the same time** | one at a time: an entry waits while a top-up works (`entry_wait_topup`), a due top-up pass waits while an entry works (`rebalance_wait_entry`) — each sizes against the book without the other's orders | same | same | same | same |
| **While a stop waits for the spread** | no entries, top-ups or repairs until it fires or is dropped | same | same | same | same |
| **Without fresh GEX data** (startup, stale snapshot) | no entries (`gex_wait`), top-ups or repairs; exits, balancing and the MM cut run | same | same | same | same |
| **MM cut** (reduce every short at market) | — | — | — | — | ✅ |
| **Churn breaker** (slot paused after 3 buy-back/re-sell round trips in 60 min) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Manual close from the monitor** (you, at market) | ⛔ (button gray) | ⛔ | ✅ only the side the trend threatens (the one the bot no longer sells); then held like a stop-loss | ⛔ unless that side is also regime-blocked | ⛔ |

Notes:

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text:
- **Stops and rolls are not blocked by any state.** Whatever the state, a leg that hits its stop, its delta exit or a roll rule is closed; only *re-selling* waits.
- **The one wait: an empty book.** When a stop triggers but the option's ask is more than 20 % above its mid, market makers have pulled their quotes, as in a flash wick, and a market buy would pay a panic price. The stop waits and is re-checked every cycle: once the spread is normal it fires if it still applies, or the leg is kept if the price came back under the stop. It never waits more than 5 minutes (`stop_spread_max_wait_minutes`), then it buys at market. The MM cut never waits.

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text: - **Top-ups back off on a book that does not trade.** A top-up that times out short is retried after 15 minutes. When 3 top-ups in a row filled nothing, nobody is trading at our price, so the wait doubles: 30 minutes, then 60 at most (2026-10-14 BTC: the same top-up was re-sent 6 times in 1.5 h, 12 orders, zero fills). A top-up that sold both its call and its put, or a confirmed limit change, starts again from 15 minutes. A top-up where only one side sold (usually the put; the other side is then sold by repair at the bid) counts as not filled, so it does not reset the wait (#98: 4 of 6 filled top-ups from 2026-10-22 to 10-28 sold the put only). Stops, exits and the MM cut never wait on it.

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text:
- **New risk is sized one step at a time.** Deribit's margin counts working orders, but the simulator the bot sizes with sees only positions. On 2026-10-15 a BTC entry and a top-up were sized in the same minutes, each ignoring the other: IM reached 25.7 % of a 20 % limit and the next pass bought the excess back, paying spread and fees twice. Now an entry waits for a working top-up and a top-up pass for a working entry — at most one order timeout (~2 min). Stops, exits, repairs and the MM cut never wait on it.
- **No order bigger than the market.** Margin alone said how much to sell, so on a large account an order could exceed a strike's whole market: on 2026-10-15 ETH offered 1,454 contracts of a call whose mainnet open interest was 164, filled 152 and sat one-legged at 1.9 % of a 20 % margin limit. Now each new leg is at most 10 % of its strike's mainnet open interest. A slot the cap leaves short of its share stays short: the rest is not re-sent (#103).
- **"Held" legs leave the strangle one-sided.** For example, a strangle whose put was stopped out keeps its call until the put can be re-sold.

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text:
- **The freeze stops new risk, not the structure.** A rolled leg is still re-sold during a freeze, because it restores a position the bot already held. A stopped leg is not.
- **Why not stop selling altogether in a negative regime?** Negative regimes are when premium is richest. In the stress test (19 paths, net of fees, vs holding), blocking every entry and top-up cost ETH 21–27 % of the result; blocking only the threatened side was +0.4–1.8 % on ETH and +20–24 % on BTC (2026-10-09).
- **Kill switch:** it cancels every order, books whatever a working entry had already filled, then buys back every short the *exchange* reports (not only those in the bot's book) and checks the account is flat.

chunks.title: 9. Market regimes and what the bot does
chunks.text: - **Restarts:** a side closed by a stop-loss, delta exit, manual close or MM cut stays held across a restart: the bot rebuilds those holds from its journal at startup, with the original time, so the 72 h cooldown keeps running. A side shed by GEX is rebuilt the same way, with the flip and buffer it was shed at, so its repair waits as it would have (before 2026-10-14 a restart forgot it: a deploy 20 minutes after a shed re-sold BTC's put a day early). The freeze and regime conditions are rebuilt from the daily closes.

chunks.title: 10. The parameters, in plain words
chunks.text:
| Setting | Shipped value | Plain meaning | Turn it up → | Turn it down → |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Slots (`dte_delta_matrix`) | BTC 25 d and 50 d, ETH 30 d and 50 d, all at 0.16 | which strangles to keep open | more positions | fewer positions |
| Entry delta | 0.16 | how far from the price to sell | closer: more premium, more risk | further: less premium, safer |
| `rollout_dte` | 15 days | when to stop holding | exits earlier, less gamma risk | holds longer, more decay, more risk |
| `roi_take_profit` | 50 % | how much profit is "enough" | holds longer for more | banks sooner, re-sells more often |
| `stop_loss_multiplier` | 2× | how much loss to tolerate | fewer stop-outs, bigger losses | more stop-outs, smaller losses |
| `delta_exit_threshold` | 0.30 | how far a move may go against a side before it is closed early (and paused like a stop) | fewer early exits, more 2× stops | more early exits, smaller losses each |
| `max_leg_size_multiple` | 2× | biggest new position vs a normal one | bigger positions when margin allows | smaller, steadier positions |
| `repair_cooldown_hours` | 72 h | how long a stopped-out side stays empty | longer pause after a loss | re-enters sooner |

chunks.title: 10. The parameters, in plain words
chunks.text:
| Setting | Shipped value | Plain meaning | Turn it up → | Turn it down → |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `delta_drift_threshold` | 0.10 | when a far leg is "dead" | refreshes legs sooner | lets legs drift further |
| `iv_margin_bands` | 50 / 35 / 20 % by DVOL band | how much of the account is at work, by market calm | larger positions | smaller positions |
| `max_mm_pct` | 35 % | safety distance from liquidation | closer to liquidation | earlier forced reductions |
| `min_premium` | 0.001 BTC / ETH | minimum price worth selling, in the coin | fewer, richer trades | more, cheaper trades |

Only these settings are in the config files. The rest — how long a new regime must last before resizing (2 daily closes), how orders are worked, the GEX confirmation counts and timers, the stop's empty-book wait, the churn breaker, expiry choice — are fixed in code since 2026-10-14 (README "Configuration" lists them), so there are fewer dials to manage; each is still re-tested in the stress tool before it changes.

chunks.title: 11. Lessons and recommendations from this study
chunks.text:
These are observations from building and reviewing the system, not trading advice.

1. **The exit plumbing matters as much as the entry idea.** The code review behind this version found several ways a "good" strategy could quietly turn dangerous: duplicate positions after rolls, legs dropped from tracking after partial fills, a kill switch that restarted itself into the market. Every one of them was in order handling, not in the trading idea.
2. **Test the backtest.** The backtest once used the computer's clock instead of the simulated date and silently made zero trades. Results that look "fine" can be meaningless. Check trade counts and sanity-check against intuition.
3. **Prefer defined risk.** An iron condor (strangle + cheaper far options bought as insurance) gives up some premium to cap the worst case. For anything beyond a study, that trade-off is usually worth it.
4. **Size for the bad month, not the average month.** A strategy that wins 85 % of the time can still lose a year's profit in one week.

chunks.title: 11. Lessons and recommendations from this study
chunks.text:
5. **Use testnet to prove mechanics, not profits.** Testnet prices are thin and sometimes synthetic; it's great for checking that fills, rolls, stops and the kill switch behave, and useless for judging returns. What evidence exists for returns: the weekly evidence report replays each bot's week on recorded mainnet books and, in its "replay vs live" section, shows how far that replay is from what the journal shows (in coin and as a % of the live result, net of fees), with the causes the journal records. A week the recorder did not fully cover is listed as not comparable rather than estimated, and a live account shows percentages only.
6. **Change one thing at a time and write down why.** Tune a parameter, record the reason and the date, and compare before/after. Otherwise you can't tell whether the change or the market made the difference.

chunks.title: 12. Glossary
chunks.text:
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ATM / OTM / ITM** | at / out of / in the money: strike at, away from, or past the current price |
| **Break-even** | the price at expiry where the trade neither gains nor loses |
| **DVOL** | Deribit's 30-day implied-volatility index for BTC/ETH |
| **IV percentile** | where today's DVOL sits versus the past year (0 = lowest, 100 = highest) |
| **GEX / gamma flip** | estimated dealer gamma exposure; the price where it changes sign. Below the flip, dealer hedging tends to amplify moves |
| **Inverse option** | an option priced and settled in the coin (BTC), not in dollars |
| **Portfolio Margin** | the exchange's margin model that nets risk across all positions |
| **Perpetual** | a futures contract without expiry, often used to hedge delta |
| **Iron condor** | a strangle plus cheaper, further-out options bought to cap the maximum loss |

<sub>Educational study of an automated trading system — not investment advice. Options trading can lose more than the premium collected; crypto markets are highly volatile.</sub>

chunks.title: `underlying` — Coin
chunks.text:
The coin this bot trades (BTC or ETH). There is one config file per coin; it names the bot rather than tunes it.

- **Range:** not checked
- **Policy:** none

chunks.title: `strategy_id` — Strategy name
chunks.text:
Names the strategy in the journal and in order labels. The shipped files leave it unset; it does not change any trading rule.

- **Range:** not checked
- **Policy:** none

chunks.title: `dte_delta_matrix[].dte` — Slot days to expiry
chunks.text:
Each slot sells one strangle on an expiry about this many days away. Longer: more premium per trade and larger moves to sit through; shorter: faster decay, more rolls and fees.

- **Range:** see "Also"
- **Unit:** days
- **Also:** above rollout_dte, or a new strangle would be rolled at once
- **Policy:** entry — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** backtest --sweep; backtest --sweep-ladders; cmd/stress -slots; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `dte_delta_matrix[].deltas[]` — Slot entry delta
chunks.text:
How far from the price each leg is sold, as option delta (0.16 is about one standard deviation away). Higher: more premium, and moves reach the strikes more often; lower: less premium, fewer stops.

- **Range:** 0.01 to 0.49 (step 0.01)
- **Unit:** delta (absolute)
- **Also:** delta_drift_threshold at most 75 % of it
- **Also:** delta_exit_threshold above it
- **Policy:** entry — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** backtest --sweep; cmd/stress -slots DTE:delta, -slotdelta; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `rollout_dte` — Roll at days to expiry
chunks.text:
A strangle is bought back when its expiry is this close, and its slot opens a new one. Higher: leaves the riskier last weeks earlier and keeps less of the time decay.

- **Range:** see "Also"
- **Unit:** days
- **Also:** below every slot's dte
- **Policy:** exits — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** backtest --sweep; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `delta_drift_threshold` — Roll when delta falls below
chunks.text:
A leg whose |delta| falls below this has little premium left: it is bought back and re-sold nearer the entry delta. Higher: rolls sooner and more often, paying spread and fees for fresher premium.

- **Range:** ≥ 0 (step 0.01)
- **Unit:** delta (absolute)
- **Also:** at most 75 % of every entry delta (config.MaxDriftToEntryRatio)
- **Policy:** exits — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/stress -drift; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `roi_take_profit` — Take profit at
chunks.text:
A leg is bought back once it has earned this share of its premium (0.50 = half) and is re-sold. Lower: takes gains sooner and trades more; higher: holds longer for the rest, exposed to moves meanwhile.

- **Range:** not checked
- **Unit:** fraction of premium
- **Policy:** exits — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** backtest --sweep; cmd/stress -tp; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `stop_loss_multiplier` — Stop-loss at
chunks.text:
A leg is bought back at market when its loss reaches this multiple of its premium (2 = twice the premium). Lower: cuts losses earlier with more stops on noise; higher: fewer stops, larger losses when one fires.

- **Range:** ≥ 0.1 (step 0.1)
- **Unit:** × premium
- **Policy:** exits — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** backtest --sweep; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `delta_exit_threshold` — Delta exit at
chunks.text:
A leg whose |delta| reaches this is bought back before the stop-loss and re-sold only after the repair cooldown. Lower: exits earlier on smaller moves; higher: waits longer, closer to the stop.

- **Range:** ≤ 0.99 (step 0.01)
- **Unit:** delta (absolute)
- **When absent:** 0.30 (also when 0)
- **Also:** above every entry delta
- **Policy:** exits — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/stress -breach; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `repair_cooldown_hours` — Repair cooldown
chunks.text:
After a stop-loss, delta exit or manual close, the leg is re-sold no sooner than this, and only while entries are not frozen and the gamma regime is not negative. Longer: less re-selling into a move, more time one-sided.

- **Range:** ≥ 0 (step 1)
- **Unit:** hours
- **When absent:** 72 (also when 0)
- **Policy:** repair — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `gamma_flip_buffer_sd` — Gamma flip buffer
chunks.text:
In a negative gamma regime a leg is shed only once spot is this many daily standard deviations beyond the gamma flip. Higher: fewer sheds and more exposure in a falling market; lower: sheds sooner and more often.

- **Range:** 0 to 3 (step 0.1)
- **Unit:** daily standard deviations
- **When absent:** 1 (also when 0)
- **Policy:** gex — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/stress -flipbufsd; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `gex_direction` — Direction source
chunks.text:
Which side to avoid in a negative gamma regime: sma (the trend of daily moving averages) or bias (spot against the gamma flip, as the reference script). It decides which legs are shed and when they are re-sold.

- **Range:** sma \| bias
- **When absent:** sma
- **Policy:** gex — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/stress -direction; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `iv_margin_bands[].min_iv_pct` — Margin band start
chunks.text:
Where a margin band starts, as the percentile of today's DVOL in the last year. With max_im_pct it sets how much initial margin the bot may use when volatility is rich or calm.

- **Range:** 0 to 100 (step 1)
- **Unit:** DVOL percentile
- **When absent:** bands 70 / 30 / 0 at 50 / 35 / 20 %
- **Also:** the lowest band starts at 0
- **Also:** no two bands start at the same percentile
- **Policy:** margin — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/stress -bands (three bands); cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `iv_margin_bands[].max_im_pct` — Margin band limit
chunks.text:
The most initial margin the bot may use in that band. Higher: larger positions and more premium, and larger losses in a move. A confirmed negative gamma regime uses the lowest band.

- **Range:** 1 to 100 (step 1)
- **Unit:** % of margin balance
- **When absent:** bands 70 / 30 / 0 at 50 / 35 / 20 %
- **Policy:** margin — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/stress -bands (three bands); cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `max_mm_pct` — Maintenance-margin limit
chunks.text:
Above this maintenance margin the bot reduces positions at market at once and opens nothing new; Deribit liquidates at 100. Higher: more room before forced cuts, less before liquidation.

- **Range:** 1 to 99 (step 1)
- **Unit:** % of margin balance
- **When absent:** 35 (also when 0)
- **Policy:** margin — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `max_leg_size_multiple` — Leg size cap
chunks.text:
A new leg is at most this many times its slot's normal size (its margin share ÷ the strangle's own margin per lot), so offsets in the book cannot inflate a size. Higher: larger legs when the book offsets them.

- **Range:** ≥ 1 (step 0.1)
- **Unit:** × normal size
- **When absent:** 2 (also when 0)
- **Policy:** sizing — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/stress -cap; cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `min_premium` — Minimum premium
chunks.text:
The least premium a leg must bring at the lowest price its order can step down to; a leg under it is not sold, and 0 accepts any. Higher: skips thin strikes, less income when premiums are low.

- **Range:** not checked
- **Unit:** coin per contract
- **Policy:** entry — a change to its default needs the product owner
- **Tested by:** cmd/compare (two configs: backtest, replay, stress)

chunks.title: `backtest.fill_model` — Backtest fill model
chunks.text:
Backtest only: mid, bid_ask or slippage. The simulator does not read it today; the trading bot never does.

- **Range:** not checked
- **Policy:** none
- **Tested by:** backtest

Backtest only: a simulated market order fills this fraction of the mid worse than the mid. No effect on trading.

- **Range:** not checked
- **Unit:** fraction of mid
- **Policy:** none
- **Tested by:** backtest

Backtest only: next_tick fills a simulated limit order on the next tick; any other value fills it at once. No effect on trading.

- **Range:** not checked

- **Tested by:** backtest

chunks.text:
Backtest only: the fee per contract as a fraction of the underlying (0.0003 = Deribit's 0.03 %), capped at 12.5 % of the price. No effect on trading.

chunks.title: Monitor guide
chunks.text:
How to read each page of the monitor. It is written for the person who owns the account, not for developers. Every page has one section below, with the same name as its item in the menu bar. The menu bar shows Overview and Details (pro) directly. Positions, Income, Worst case, Activity and Account are under **Operational**, and How it works is under **Help**.

Three rules hold on every page. Amounts are in the bot's coin first (BTC for the BTC bot, ETH for the ETH bot) and in US dollars second, as a smaller "about" figure. Different coins are never added together. A figure the monitor does not have says "unknown" or "not yet" and gives the reason; it never shows a zero in its place.

Every figure is a fact from the bot's journal or from Deribit, or a labelled estimate. Nothing here is a forecast or advice.

chunks.title: Overview
chunks.text:
The first page. It answers one question: is the bot running, and how is it doing this month?

**The status line** at the top says whether each bot is trading ("Both trading · updated 14:02"). Under it, an amber line appears for each bot that holds something back, in plain words. Example: "ETH sells no new puts: negative gamma regime in a bear trend". Amber means the bot is waiting on purpose, not that it is broken.

**The four tiles**:
- *Coins earned this month*: the money kept after closes, net of Deribit fees. It counts only positions already closed.
- *Open now*: the profit or loss of positions still open. It is not realised until they close and can change every minute.
- *Worst case*: the loss of one very bad day, as an estimate. The Worst case page explains it.
- *Margin used*: how much of the margin limit the bot has used. The bar shows the limit; the footer shows the room left.

**The profit and loss chart** has two switches: Coin or USD, and 1 day, 1 week or 1 month. The solid line is total profit and loss, including open positions. The dashed grey line is realised only. A loss is shown in red and with a minus sign.

chunks.title: Overview
chunks.text:
**One band per bot** shows a header with the coin, the price, the gamma regime (positive or negative), the trend (bull, bear or neutral), how old the last GEX reading is, and the margin bar. Below it, a price chart with 60 daily candles: green for up days, grey for down days. Red is kept for losses only. The shaded corridor lies between the lowest and the highest strike the bot has sold. The dashed lines are the sold strikes, SMA9 and SMA21, the swing high and low, and the gamma flip with its shed band. Each can be switched off with its button. On the right, one row for each strangle: its slot, expiry, days left, profit and loss in coin, and how much of the premium has been kept. A click opens its payoff chart.

**The last trade** sits under each band: when it happened and what the bot sold or bought back. One click on *Why?* opens the reason the bot recorded in its journal when it traded. For a buy-back it also shows that trade's past result, net of fees, in coin and USD. A past result is no promise of future results. *All actions, explained* opens the Activity page.

chunks.title: Overview
chunks.text:
**When the bot holds nothing**, the band says "Nothing held" and the *Open now* and *Worst case* tiles say "nothing open" instead of a zero.

**Colours and marks**:
- A dimmed band means the bot's data is stale; the age of the last answer is shown.
- "GEX 40s ago" turns amber after five minutes. Until the GEX reading is fresh again, the bot opens nothing new.
- A bot that is down says so on its band.

**When something looks wrong**:
- Stale data or a bot down: look at the header chips (STALE, OFFLINE, LOOP STALLED, HALTED). LOOP STALLED means the page answers but the bot's decision loop has not run for three intervals, so exits are not being checked.
- A held leg: the amber line names the rule. Open Positions or Details (pro), Missing legs, to see when it is released.
- A loss: open Activity for the bot's own sentence on each close, then Details (pro) for the rule and numbers.

Learn more: glossary terms *gamma regime*, *trend*, *freeze*, *margin*; OptionStrategy.md sections 3, 8 and 9.

chunks.title: Income
chunks.text:
Month by month, where the money came from. It reads the journal's closes, after fees.

**Four tiles**: *Last 6 months, after fees*; *Average month* (with how many months were up and down); *Worst month*; *Worst week* (as a share of the account). A switch changes the amounts between the coin and USD.

**The table** has one row per UTC month, newest first:
- *Paid to you*: the premium received when the options were sold.
- *Paid to buy back*: what it cost to close them.
- *Exchange fees*: Deribit's fees, shown as a negative number.
- *Result*: paid to you, minus buy-back, minus fees.
- *Holding alone*: what the same coin would have gained or lost if it had only been held. In the coin it is 0 by definition; in USD it is the price change.

A month with a loss is tinted and marked "loss". A month without closes says "no closes". The current month says "so far".

**When something looks wrong**: a loss month is normal data, not an error; the table keeps it in the open. "Unknown" in *holding alone* means the price for that month was not recorded. Testnet income is practice money, not real income.

chunks.title: Income
chunks.text: Learn more: glossary terms *income over months*, *worst month*, *worst week*, *premium*, *exchange fees*; OptionStrategy.md section 4.

chunks.title: Worst case
chunks.text:
An estimate of what one very bad day would cost the positions held right now. It is a model, not a measurement and not a forecast.

**The headline** is the worse of the two big-move days (down and up), as a loss in coin, in USD and as a share of the account.

**The five rows** show what different days would do: a very bad fall (−3 daily standard deviations), a bad fall (−2), a quiet day (0), a strong rise (+2) and a very strong rise (+3). Each row has the price move in percent, how big that is in typical daily swings, and the result with its sign, in coin and USD. A typical daily swing comes from DVOL, the market's own measure of expected volatility.

No row says how often such a day happens. The model understates how large crypto moves can be, and there is no measured figure.

**What the bot does on a bad day** is shown beside it: it closes a leg when its price reaches the stop-loss multiple of what it was sold for. A stop is a trigger, and a fast move can fill it at a worse price than the stop level.

chunks.title: Worst case
chunks.text:
**When something looks wrong**: "unknown" means the model could not run, for example no position is held or DVOL is missing; the reason is written next to it. A stale page keeps the last figures and says "Not updating".

Learn more: glossary terms *worst case*, *stop-loss*, *DVOL*, *delta exit*; OptionStrategy.md sections 6 and 8.

chunks.title: Positions
chunks.text:
One card for each strangle the bot holds: a put and a call sold on the same expiry. Cards are ordered by slot, shortest first.

**The card** has a title (coin, slot in days, expiry), the time of its data and the **premium earned so far**: a bar and words such as "62 % of the premium earned". A negative share means the position is at a loss.

**The payoff chart**: the horizontal axis is the coin's price; the vertical axis is profit and loss in coin.
- The dashed curve is the result on the expiry date.
- The solid curve is the result if the position were bought back now, from a model.
- Green fill is a gain. Hatched fill is a loss. Hatching is used so the loss does not rely on colour alone.
- The "now" marker shows today's price and the position's result at that price.
- Vertical lines mark the strikes (the *floor* is the put, the *ceiling* is the call), the break-evens at expiry, each leg's exit line (where its delta would reach the delta-exit threshold) and each leg's stop-loss level. Each kind has a button to hide it.

**The delta box** gives the strangle's net delta in coin and in USD for a 1 % move, then each leg's. A negative delta means the position gains if the price falls.

chunks.title: Positions
chunks.text:
**When something looks wrong**:
- A card that says a side is missing ("no call held: repair waiting") has one leg only. The reason in brackets is the rule that holds the repair: a stop cooldown, a GEX shed, the confirmed regime side, or the margin limit.
- "Unknown" in the today curve means an implied volatility was missing for a leg. The expiry curve is still drawn.

Learn more: glossary terms *strangle*, *break-even*, *exit line*, *delta*, *stop-loss*, *missing leg*, *repair*; OptionStrategy.md sections 3, 4 and 5.

chunks.title: How it works
chunks.text:
The bot's method in three pictures, using the strangle you hold. If none is held, an example is shown and is labelled as an example.

**1. One position, two legs**: the put (the floor) and the call (the ceiling), each with its strike, what it commits to on the expiry date and the premium paid now, in coin.

**2. What you end with on the expiry date**: a chart of the result at expiry. Between the strikes, all the premium is kept. Beyond a break-even, a loss grows; that zone is hatched. The dashed line is today's price.

**3. How the bot defends the position**: four cards, in the order the rules are applied:
- *Take profit*: buy back when enough of the premium has been kept.
- *Exit line*: buy back when a leg's delta reaches the delta-exit threshold, because the move looks real.
- *Stop-loss*: buy back at market when the price of the option reaches the stop multiple.
- *Wait, then repair*: after a stop, the bot waits the repair cooldown before it sells that side again.

**When something looks wrong**: "exit lines move with the market (unknown …)" means the model has no volatility figure at the moment. The explanations are the same words as the glossary.

chunks.title: How it works
chunks.text: Learn more: glossary terms *premium*, *delta*, *strike*, *expiry*, *margin*; OptionStrategy.md sections 1 to 4.

chunks.title: Activity
chunks.text:
What the bot did and why, in plain sentences, from its own journal. Entries are grouped by day (Today, Yesterday, then dates), and the time is in 24-hour format.

**The filters**:
- *Everything*.
- *Money in or out*: opens and closes.
- *Protection*: stop-loss, delta exit, GEX shed, maintenance-margin cut, kill switch, manual close, freezes and every action by a person.
- *Waiting*: skips and holds, such as waiting for fresh GEX, a repair held after a stop, or no free expiry.

**Each entry** has a time, an icon with a text name, a bold first line and the rest of the sentence. An arrow down is money in (an option sold). An arrow up is a buy-back. A shield is protection. A clock is waiting. A person is an action by a person, with their name and role. Opens show *Paid to you*; closes show *Result*, both in coin, signed.

**When something looks wrong**: a long run of Waiting entries means a rule is holding the bot back; the sentence names it. "Show earlier days" adds three more days. An empty journal says so. The raw entries, with all their numbers, are under Details (pro).

Learn more: glossary terms *skipped*, *hold*, *freeze*, *shed*, *kill switch*; OptionStrategy.md section 9.

chunks.title: Account
chunks.text:
The account as Deribit reports it, plus the margin policy each bot applies. Figures here are Deribit's; the monitor does not recompute them.

**Account totals**: the margin model, whether cross collateral is on, and equity, margin balance, initial margin (IM) and maintenance margin (MM) in USD, with IM and MM bars. A bar turns amber from half of its limit and red from four fifths. Deribit liquidates positions when MM reaches 100 %. Then one block per asset: balance, equity, available, withdrawable and reserved.

**Margin policy per bot**:
- IM used against the active limit, and why that limit applies (the DVOL band, or a negative gamma regime).
- MM used against its limit.
- Whether new entries are allowed or frozen, with the reason.
- Any pending limit change with its countdown, for example "1 of 2 daily closes".

chunks.title: Account
chunks.text:
**The Rebalance button** resizes the positions towards the current limit. A dry run shows the plan and sends nothing. A real run asks for confirmation, and only a manager or an admin may run it. When IM is over the limit by 1.5 points or less and the limit has not changed, the plan buys nothing back: that is market drift, and the positions are shown as kept. Further over, it buys back toward the limit as before.

**Not managed by the bot** lists any other position on the account, for example one bought by hand. No bot trades these, but they use margin, so they are shown.

**Privacy** has your switch for the monthly question in the assistant. It is off after you choose "Don't ask me again"; turn it back on here.

**When something looks wrong**:
- "IM over limit since …" means margin used is above the limit. The bot only warns; it sells and buys nothing to correct it by itself.
- "Frozen" means new risk waits for a limit change to be confirmed on daily closes. Exits and repairs continue.
- STALE or a failed poll means the figures are old.

Learn more: glossary terms *margin*, *IM limit*, *MM limit*, *freeze*, *rebalance*, *IM over limit*; OptionStrategy.md section 8.

chunks.title: Details (pro)
chunks.text:
The numbers page for an active trader. Figures come first and graphics are small. All figures are in coin first, with USD smaller beside them.

**The top line** counts bots online, orders sent and filled, closes and entries skipped, since a date. The **section bar** jumps to Positions, Missing legs, Trades, Working orders and Not managed. A section is amber when it needs attention.

**Open positions**: one line per leg, grouped by strangle. Columns include quantity, entry and mark prices, *premium kept*, profit and loss, |Δ| against the exit line (amber from 80 % of the threshold), distance out of the money, the stop level and the greeks. *Close…* appears only where the manual-close rule allows it: a leg on the side the confirmed regime blocks.

**Missing legs**: one row for each one-legged strangle. It shows who holds the repair (a stop, a GEX shed, the regime side), the market now and when the hold ends.

**Trades and results**: realised profit and loss per coin, the win rate, average win against average loss, results by exit reason and by slot, and one line per trade. A caret opens the rule and its numbers. *Why?* on a row asks the assistant to explain it.

chunks.title: Details (pro)
chunks.text:
**Working orders**: orders still resting, with fill progress and time left before the fill timeout.

**When something looks wrong**: a working order past its fill timeout, or a position no bot manages, turns its section amber. A loss is red and is never hidden.

Learn more: glossary terms *premium kept*, *delta exit*, *stop hold*, *working order*, *win rate*, *avg win*, *avg loss*; OptionStrategy.md sections 4, 6 and 9.

chunks.title: The assistant
chunks.text:
The **Ask** button at the bottom right of every page opens a panel. You write a question; it answers from the published help (the strategy guide, this guide, the settings reference and the glossary) and from the bot's journal of the last seven days.

**How to read an answer**: each answer lists its sources as chips. A chip opens the document section, the glossary term or the trade in Details (pro). Check the source: answers can be wrong. The line under the answer says whether it came from the help, from your journal, or was refused.

**What it will not do**: it gives no advice and no forecasts. It says "I don't know" when the sources do not cover the question. A question about money or timing, such as "should I close this?" or "where will the price go?", is refused. It answers in its own words and never just sends you to read a document. When it cannot back an answer with the bot's records and the help, it says it couldn't confirm an answer and won't guess.

**Why?** buttons on trade rows (Details and Activity) ask for the reason behind one trade, using the facts the journal recorded for it: the rule, its numbers, the instrument, the time and the market then.

chunks.title: The assistant
chunks.text:
**A question from the team**: about once a month, a "1" on the Ask button means one optional question is waiting: how likely you are to recommend the monitor, from 0 to 10. A score of 9 or 10 asks what we do best; 0 to 8 asks what to improve first. A comment is optional and stays private with your account. "Not now" or × closes it until next month; "Don't ask me again" turns it off (Account, Privacy turns it back on). It appears only if you said yes to usage analytics, and never in your first 14 days. The assistant works the same whether you answer or not.

**Limits and flags**: each person has a number of questions an hour, shown under the box. *Flag* marks an answer for review. Questions and answers are logged for review, never the account's keys.

chunks.title: The assistant
chunks.text:
**How to report a bug or ask for a feature**: describe it in the Ask box with what you saw, where (the page, the bot and the time) and the evidence (a number, a journal entry or the steps to see it again). When something is missing, the assistant lists what to add. When it has enough, it shows a draft request, a bug or an enhancement. Nothing is sent until you press *Send for review*; *Edit* changes any field and *Discard* drops it. A sent request goes to a private review queue, not to the public repository, and amounts, account details and personal data are removed before anything is made public. Each person may send 10 requests a day.

**My requests**: the tab in the Ask panel lists the requests you sent, newest first, with their status (In review, Filed, Fixed, Not planned, Not a bug, Duplicate or Needs info) and the team's note. You see only your own.

**When something looks wrong**: a dimmed Ask button means the assistant is off or not set up; hover for the reason. "Retry" appears when a request failed.

chunks.title: The assistant
chunks.text: Learn more: OptionStrategy.md section 12; the glossary. Features that are not menu pages (the survey, sign-in, consent, roles, environments, videos and the admin pages) are described in the sections below.

chunks.title: The monthly survey
chunks.text:
The survey is one optional question in the Ask panel: how likely you are to recommend the monitor, from 0 to 10. This is the NPS survey.

**How to answer the NPS survey**: when it is due, a "1" shows on the Ask button. Open Ask and the question is the first card. Pick a number from 0 to 10. A score of 9 or 10 then asks what we do best. A score of 0 to 8 asks what to improve first. Choose from the short list of reasons and add a comment if you want; the comment is optional and stays private with your account. The answer never includes amounts.

**How to skip the survey**: "Not now" or × closes it until next month. "Don't ask me again" turns it off. Account, Privacy has a switch that turns it back on. The assistant works the same whether you answer or not.

**Is my survey answer in the audit trail?** Only the fact that you answered, and which survey, with your username and the time. Your score, reasons and comment are not in it. Turning the survey off or back on is recorded the same way.

chunks.title: The monthly survey
chunks.text:
**When it shows**: at most once every 30 days, counted from the day it was shown, answered or not. It shows only when you said yes to usage analytics, only after your account is 14 days old and you have signed in at least 3 times, and not while a bot's last 7 days is a net loss or cannot be read.

**Can I open the survey myself?** No. You cannot trigger it on demand: it appears once every 30 days when you have agreed to analytics. When it is due you can still answer it in the Ask panel, or skip it.

Learn more: "Analytics and your consent" and "The assistant" in this guide.

chunks.title: The four answers questions
chunks.text:
The four answers questions are two optional questions in the Ask panel: what you came to check today, and what was hardest to find. Each offers the same five choices: what it holds, making or losing, the worst case, why the last trade, or none of these.

**How to answer the four answers questions**: when they are due, a "1" shows on the Ask button. Open Ask and the questions are the first card. Pick one choice for either question, or for both, and press Send. You can leave one blank. There is no text box, and the answer never includes amounts.

**How to skip the four answers questions**: "Not now" or × closes the card. Closing the Ask panel without answering skips it too. It is not asked again for 30 days.

**When the four answers questions show**: at most once every 30 days, counted from the day they were shown, answered or not. They show only when you said yes to usage analytics, only after your account is 14 days old and you have signed in at least 3 times. They never show in the same session as the monthly survey, nor within 7 days after it. Once shown on one device or tab, they do not show on another.

chunks.title: The four answers questions
chunks.text: Learn more: "The monthly survey" and "Analytics and your consent" in this guide.

chunks.title: Sign-in and password
chunks.text:
You sign in at the sign-in page with a username and password. Every page and every part of the monitor needs a signed-in session; without one you are sent to the sign-in page. A session is kept alive while you use the monitor and ends after 14 days or when you sign out.

**How to change your password**: choose Change password in the account menu. Enter the current password and the new one twice. The new one must differ from the current one and be at least 12 characters. Your sessions on other devices end when you change it.

**How to reset a forgotten password**: ask an admin. An admin issues a single-use reset link on the Users page. Open the link, choose a new password and sign in with it. The link works once and then stops working.

**Signed out everywhere**: a password change, a password reset, a role change or the deletion of your account signs you out on every device. Sign in again to continue.

Learn more: "Roles" in this guide.

chunks.title: Deleting your account
chunks.text:
You can delete your own monitor account at any time, whatever your role.

**How to delete my account**: choose Delete my account in the account menu. The first screen says what is deleted: your sign-in, your usage analytics events and your survey answers, with any text you wrote. It cannot be undone. Press Continue, then Delete my account.

**What deleting my account does not touch**: your exchange accounts and funds. The bots keep trading, and deposits and withdrawals stay on the exchange.

**The question before you go**: below the delete button, one optional question asks the main reason you leave. Pick a reason, or Other with a few words if you want. Skip and delete, or ×, deletes the account at once without an answer; so does Delete my account with nothing picked. The answer is kept only if you said yes to usage analytics, and it is deleted with your account. Escape or Back returns to the first screen without deleting.

**Why can't I delete my account as an admin?** The monitor always keeps one admin. If you are the only admin, make another person an admin on the Users page first, then delete your account.

Learn more: "Analytics and your consent" in this guide.

chunks.title: Roles
chunks.text:
There are three roles. A **user** may see every page. A **manager** may do what a user does and also close a leg by hand and rebalance by hand, including the dry run. An **admin** may do what a manager does and also use the admin pages: Users, Audit and Analytics.

**Who can rebalance?** Managers and admins. Closing a leg by hand is the same. A user may still see the buttons, but the monitor refuses the action and the bot receives nothing. The role is checked each time you act, so a role change takes effect at once.

**Is every action checked and recorded?** Yes. Every action that changes something is checked on the server against your role, whatever the page shows: the wrong role is refused and nothing changes. An allowed action is recorded in the audit trail with your username, the action and the time.

Each environment has its own people and roles.

Learn more: "Sign-in and password" and "For admins" in this guide.

chunks.title: Analytics and your consent
chunks.text:
The monitor collects usage analytics only if you say yes. Your answer is stored with your account. Until you answer, or if you say no, nothing is collected.

**What the monitor collects about me**: which pages and features are used and how (for example that a help video was played), under a random session code. Events outside a fixed list are refused. **What it does not collect**: no keys, no passwords, no amounts, no positions, no orders and no text you type in the assistant.

**How to say yes or no**: in Account, Privacy. Saying no stops collection at once. Every change of your answer is recorded in the audit trail.

**What happens to events already stored**: they stay until you ask for their deletion. Deletion on request is done by the team; ask an admin.

Learn more: "The monthly survey" in this guide.

chunks.title: Which environment you are looking at
chunks.text:
Each environment is a separate monitor with its own bot, Deribit account, people and passwords. The header shows which one you are in. **Stable** is the release track, where a tagged version runs. **mvp** runs the newest version of the code, where changes are tried first. A **testnet** label means the bot trades on Deribit's test exchange with test money, not real capital. Numbers from the two environments are never added together.

Learn more: OptionStrategy.md section 12.

chunks.title: How-to videos
chunks.text:
Short how-to videos explain one task each: reading the summary card, one position and the worst case, why the last trade, the margin bar, why entries are frozen, closing a leg by hand, previewing a rebalance, and income month by month. They run 45 to 75 seconds and have captions. They are planned: none plays in the monitor yet.

Learn more: "The assistant" in this guide.

chunks.title: For admins
chunks.text:
These pages are for the admin role only. A manager or a user who opens one is refused.

**Users**: lists the people of this environment with role, email, when created and last sign-in. An admin creates a user (a username of 3 to 64 letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens, and a password of at least 12 characters), changes a role, resets a password, issues a single-use reset link, signs a person out everywhere, or deletes a user. Every change signs that person out everywhere. There is always at least one admin, and you cannot delete yourself.

**Audit**: the trail of who did what: sign-ins, user changes, role changes, consent changes, closes and rebalances by hand, and survey answers (which survey only, never the answer). It is read-only.

**Analytics**: the weekly usage report (Usage), built only from the events of people who said yes. A Delivery view is not on the page yet.

Learn more: "Roles" and "Analytics and your consent" in this guide.

chunks.title: Notifications
chunks.text:
The **bell** in the menu bar, before your name, lists what happened to your book and your requests, and what waits for you. On a phone it opens the Notifications page.

**Needs you** (counted on the bell): a short question from the team is waiting, or a request you sent needs more from you. Their buttons open the question or My requests in the assistant.

**Updates** (listed, never counted): what the bot did to your book on the page's bot (a stop-loss, a delta exit, the kill switch, a sell cancelled because new risk is frozen, initial margin over the limit), each with the journal's plain sentence and *Why?*; the status of your requests (accepted as a public issue, declined with its reason, shipped); and one What's new note per release. Fills and skips are never notifications.

**Reading**: an unread item has a dot and bold text. Following an item marks it read; "Mark all read" marks the whole list. Read marks are kept with your account, so your other devices agree. Items are kept 90 days.

chunks.title: Notifications
chunks.text:
**Settings**: the Notifications page turns each kind of update off or on. What needs you cannot be turned off; the question from the team has its own "Don't ask me again". Nothing is sent by e-mail or to your phone.

**When something looks wrong**: if the bot does not answer, the list says its events could not be read and still shows the rest.

chunks.title: action funnel
chunks.text:
Each step of a manual close or rebalance, from opening the dialog to confirming, with how many times it happened.

Analytics page (admins only). The manual close and rebalance cards list each step people took that week: the dialog opened, cancelled or confirmed. A big gap between opened and confirmed shows where people stop.

A confirmed step sends real orders to a bot; the card only counts them.

chunks.title: actions
chunks.text:
What an admin can do to a person: reset the password, send a reset link, sign them out everywhere, or delete them.

Users page (admins only). Reset password sets a new one and signs the person out on every browser. Reset link makes a link, valid once for 30 minutes, with which the person chooses their own new password. Sign out everywhere ends every session. Delete removes the person and their analytics events. Each asks for a confirmation first. You cannot delete or reset yourself here.

None on trading: none of these changes a position or an order.

chunks.title: active people
chunks.text:
How many different people used the monitor in a period. Each person counts once, however often they came.

Analytics page (admins only). The weekly usage report counts each person once per period, shown for this week, the last 30 days and by role. It keeps a scrambled code per person, never a name or email, and shows counts only. Only people who agreed to analytics are counted.

A count of people, not of money: it says nothing about how the bots trade.

chunks.title: age
chunks.text:
How long an order has been working.

The time since the order was placed. The bot re-prices it as it ages and cancels it at the fill timeout.

None by itself.

chunks.title: asset
chunks.text:
A coin held in the account (e.g. BTC, ETH, USDC).

The account can hold several coins. Each one counts toward the margin balance at its value.

None by itself.

chunks.title: available
chunks.text:
Money free to back new positions or orders.

Available is the margin balance minus the initial margin already in use.

Less available means less room for new positions.

chunks.title: avg loss
chunks.text:
The average loss of the closes that lost money.

The mean result, after fees, of losing closes, in dollars. For option sellers it is often several times the average win.

A large average loss can erase many small wins.

chunks.title: avg win
chunks.text:
The average profit of the closes that made money.

The mean result, after fees, of winning closes, in dollars.

Compare it with the average loss.

chunks.title: backtest
chunks.text:
Settings for the backtest, which replays past prices; they do not affect live trading.

The backtest runs the bot's rules on past data to study them. These settings only say how its simulated fills and costs work. Past results do not predict future ones.

None on the live account.

chunks.title: backtest.commission_per_contract
chunks.text:
Backtest setting: the exchange fee rate per contract, as a fraction of the coin price (0.0003 = 0.03 %).

Backtest setting: each simulated fill pays this fraction of the coin price per contract, capped at 12.5 % of the option price, like Deribit's fee.

None on the live account; higher fees lower backtest results.

chunks.title: backtest.fill_model
chunks.text:
Backtest setting: the fill model to simulate (mid, bid_ask or slippage); the backtest does not read it today.

Backtest setting kept in the files for a choice of fill model. Today the backtest fills market orders at the middle price moved by slippage_pct, and limit orders at their limit price, whatever this says.

None on the live account.

chunks.title: backtest.limit_fill_rule
chunks.text:
Backtest setting: when a simulated limit order fills (next_tick).

Backtest setting: next_tick fills a limit order on the next price record that reaches its price.

None on the live account.

chunks.title: backtest.margin_call_liquidation
chunks.text:
Backtest setting: meant to close every simulated position when margin runs out; the backtest does not read it today.

Backtest setting kept in the files. It is meant to make the simulation close all positions when the account would be liquidated. The current backtest does not use it.

None on the live account.

chunks.title: backtest.slippage_pct
chunks.text:
Backtest setting: how much worse than the middle price a simulated market order fills, as a fraction.

Backtest setting: a simulated market buy fills this fraction above the middle price, a sale this fraction below it. 0.001 is 0.1 %.

None on the live account; more slippage gives more cautious backtest results.

chunks.title: balance
chunks.text:
How much of a coin the account holds, before open positions are valued.

The balance is the coin held in the account. Equity adds the value of open positions to it.

None by itself.

chunks.title: balance legs
chunks.text:
Buying back the extra size of the larger leg so the call and put match.

A strangle is balanced only when its call and put are the same size. If one leg is larger, for example after a partial fill, the bot buys back the difference on the larger side. It does this even during a freeze, because it lowers risk.

It removes one-sided risk and the income of the extra size.

chunks.title: bias
chunks.text:
The direction read from spot against the gamma flip: up, down or neutral.

The bias is another way to read direction. In a negative regime, spot more than the buffer above the gamma flip is 'bias up', more than the buffer below is 'bias down', otherwise neutral. The bot records both bias and trend and uses the one its settings name (gex_direction).

Under the bias, a rally through the flip sheds calls; it has shed more often than the trend in tests.

chunks.title: bid / ask
chunks.text:
The best price a buyer offers (bid) and the best price a seller asks (ask).

The bid is the highest price someone will pay now; the ask is the lowest price someone will sell for. The gap between them is the spread. The bot sells near the ask and, for most exits, buys back between the two or at the ask.

A wide spread costs more on every trade, which lowers net income.

chunks.title: bot
chunks.text:
One running copy of the strategy, trading one coin (BTC or ETH).

Each bot trades one coin on its own Deribit account and reports to the monitor. 'Bots online' counts the bots that answered recently.

None by itself.

chunks.title: buy back
chunks.text:
Buying an option the bot sold, to close it.

To end a sold option before expiry, the bot buys the same option back. The difference between the premium received and the buy-back price, after fees, is the result.

The cheaper the buy-back, the more of the premium is kept.

chunks.title: call
chunks.text:
An option that pays its buyer when the coin rises above the strike price.

A call option gives its buyer the right to buy the coin at the strike price. It gains value when the coin rises above the strike. The bot sells calls: it keeps the premium if the coin stays below the strike, and loses when the coin rises far above it.

A sold call earns its premium in a flat or falling market and loses money in a strong rise.

chunks.title: cancelled
chunks.text:
An order taken off the exchange before it filled, in whole or in part.

The bot cancels orders that did not fill in time, and orders a freeze or a shed makes unwanted. Whatever filled before the cancel is kept and tracked.

None for the unfilled part.

chunks.title: change failure rate
chunks.text:
The share of deploys that failed: rolled back, a deploy-failed issue, a revert or a bug a PR caused.

Analytics page, Delivery (DORA) topic (admins only). One of the four DORA numbers: failed deploys of all attempts in the week. Each failure counts once. NO FAILURE means nothing failed and there are too few deploys for a band yet.

A failed deploy on mvp is caught on the test account; on stable it reaches production, so both are shown apart.

chunks.title: churn pause
chunks.text:
A slot that buys back and re-sells 3 times within 60 minutes is paused for an hour.

If a slot keeps buying back and selling again, something is wrong and every round trip pays fees and the spread. After 3 round trips in 60 minutes, the slot stops opening, repairing and resizing for an hour. Exits still run.

It stops fees and spread from eating the income in a loop.

chunks.title: close
chunks.text:
Buying back a sold option, which ends that leg's position.
